title: Do people still use RM2k or RM2k3?

posts.author: ZENWARECO
posts.body:
Does anyone even use RPG Maker 2000 and 2003 anymore?   Seems like a redundant question.  I was doing a couple games and I was thinking about releasing them when they're done, but a lot of people seems like everyone is XP all the way to MV.  People just kinda think:
Oh, it's 2000 and 2003.
Outdated.
Yet I've exhausted a lot of energy into a couple games done in these.  I mean really. REALLY.
What does the Rm community think?

posts.author: Kes
posts.body:
Ara Fell was made in 2k3, and was hugely successful.  Even when it was remade in Unity, they kept the original maps and graphics.  But that was a solidly built game.
As with any other engine (not just RM), you can produce an excellent game or a piece of garbage.
What helped with Ara Fell and other 2k3 games which remain playable is that they used the REFMAP tilesets and characters, which helped the visuals enormously.  They also had a trailer which showcased the extraordinary things that 2k3 can do - iff you can event well.
In order to answer this thread, I went into my Steam version, selected 'Legacy' and played through a bit of the original build.  It ran fine on my 2-year old laptop.  I have also replayed a couple of 2k3 games over the last year or so, and had no problems.
Maybe (just guessing here) because everything has to be done through eventing, you've got to pay a lot of attention to make sure you're not building in lag.  Perhaps the lag which some have experienced is due to that, rather than the engine in itself?

posts.author: Litningman06
posts.body:
Whoa! A thread just for me! Yeah, I use 2k3. Exclusively. I started out using MV, but then I switched to XP, because I didn’t really like a couple of things about MV, and then about a year after I switched to XP, I started using 2k3 and found it was my favourite.
Personally, I work very well within limitations. All of the tools I’ve used to create my game are very outdated and limiting, but it’s fighting those limitations and finding out what I can do beyond them is why I love this specific version of the maker so much.
Finding creative solutions for engine-induced problems is extremely gratifying.

posts.author: Jollo
posts.body:
I mean everyone likes different things. I also like the old versions still, but I moved on to MZ because I wanted some modern features, higher resolution and better compatibility.
But I understand. Restrictions can really boost creativity and it's always fun to overcome hurdles and limitations. So if it is the most fun for you to work with those old engine, then go ahead. But if you want your players not to get too frustrated I would suggest using a modern version and just set the restrictions to yourself (set the tile and scree resolution, don't install plugins and so on).
